utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are just two of us today. The Asian element is missing.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not yet, yes. And I actually am invoking the provisions of the rules which enable us to sit today just the two of us. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours, this is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Are you receiving interpretation in the language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I am getting the interpretation in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If there is any problem at any time let me know, Mr. Brdjanin. Please sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Anna Richterova, assisted by Denise Gustin case manager. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, too. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman with Aleksandar Vujic for Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Good morning to you, too. Any preliminaries? I suppose no. Nothing. Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Hopefully you will be out of this courtroom within a relatively short time. Let's hope so. It also depends on how short your answers will be. So before we proceed, may I ask you to repeat your solemn undertaking, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dodik, please take a chair and Mr. Ackerman will proceed with and conclude his cross-examination. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When we broke yesterday I was getting ready to talk to you a little bit about media. We've heard a great deal about the radio and television and newspapers that were controlled by Serbs. I wonder if you ever had occasion during 1991 and 1992 to listen to any, read any of the media from Croatian or Muslim sources?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said earlier on that the media acted as propaganda of the ruling structure on all sides. This was almost the rule. I did have occasion to hear Croatian and Bosnian reports, and the programmes were designed virtually in an identical fashion, even though the contents differed of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did the Croatian or Muslim media use any kind of derogatory terminology to describe Serbs during that period?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was customary. All three sides used derogatory terms to describe the others. The Serbs called the Bosniaks Turks, the Croats Ustashas, and the Croatian and Bosniak sides called the Serbs Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You said at one point this: You said: "We could not trust the Muslims living amongst us because it was only a matter of time before they would join the Muslim forces."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could I have the page of the LiveNote?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think it's in the LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that. I didn't say that anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just see if I can find where I got it. I got it from -- I thought it was in your recorded interview, but it's not.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is an absolute misinterpretation. I couldn't possibly have made such a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I trust you with regard to what you're saying right now. I really do. I will just tell you that I have the investigator's notes from your various interviews with Mr. Tieger. And I can only tell you what the note says. "The idea that was explicitly expressed" --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Page please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 8 next to the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "The idea that was explicitly expressed was that Serbs must live in continuous territories, that they must stick to each other. We could not trust the Muslims living amongst us because it was only a matter of time before they would join the Muslim forces." Now, that's what the investigator reports that you said, but of course it's your position that you did not say that and I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought we had cleared up the matter of these notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please understand that I am only referring to these notes to ask you if in fact you said some of the things that are reported to have been said by you here, not to suggest that you did or to accuse you in any way of saying these things. But that's one of the sources of information I have, and that's what I'm doing with it. Do you understand what I mean?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did talk to Mr. Tieger and other gentlemen, and I presented certain assessments which I'm ready to repeat here. However, certain things that appeared in those documents could be due to poor interpretation or something else. In any event, please feel free to ask me anything you wish and I will give you my answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the witness is being very frank and very reasonable, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do too, and I fully accept what he's saying, fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I also have some investigator's notes of a conversation you had with Ms. Korner. You know that I've got the notes from your conversations with Tieger and from Korner and the notes that were made by investigators during those conversations. Now, I think this particular issue, you even alluded to in your testimony yesterday, but I'm not certain about that. But at page 2, Ms. Korner, of the notes of your conversation with Mr. Dodik, there appears language that: "Karadzic stated publicly that he wanted activity of the ARK stopped. He was in conflict with the people here in Banja Luka. They became renegades and not under Radovan Karadzic's control, as they wanted the national and political power here."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm sorry. I'm going to interrupt again. I do think selective quotations from a full answer is not on. In order for the witness fully to understand the context of what he said, I think the rest should be read. I know Mr. Ackerman will say I can read it, but I think that's wrong in principle. I think if he wants to read that, he should read the full answer because there is further answer on the same topic. At page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no desire to read any more than I read. That's the part I'm interested in directing to the witness' --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Provided the witness has in front of him the text of the investigator's notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I doubt that -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have the text, so I cannot comment on it. But in answer to your question, that is, whether the leadership in Krajina was to some extent in political conflict with Karadzic and his structure, I can say it was, and this is common knowledge. And there is no need to keep coming back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My real question was: Do you recall Karadzic saying publicly that he wanted the activity of ARK stopped. And if you do recall that, can you recall about when he said that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was at a parliamentary session of Bosnia and Herzegovina which was being held on the same day or about the same day, that is what he said. Now, what he did after that, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The same day as what? I mean, can you get us some kind of a time fix on it? Was it in 1992 sometime or when?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was at the beginning of 1992 but I can't tell you exactly, but I do know that it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, I am finished with any reference to any of these notes, so we don't have to worry about that anymore. I want to talk just very briefly, we should get through this fairly quickly --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I'm not worried. But I have really come here to tell the Court what I have to say and there is no need for you to keep referring me back to those notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I'm going to talk to you a little bit about some of your testimony yesterday, and I think we can probably get through this fairly rapidly. Page 20, line 15 of yesterday's LiveNote: "SDA had a Patriotic League preparing for an armed conflict." Can you tell us about when you became aware that there was a Patriotic League preparing for an armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The armed conflict engaged in by the Patriotic League occurred first in Bosanski Brod. I think it was in February, 1992. But there was awareness of the existence of the Patriotic League as early as the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And did that include an awareness that they were preparing for an armed conflict? That's the -- that's kind of the heart of my question.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was talk of the Patriotic League. I can only say, as an assumption, that it could be felt in the air, that the ruling parties at the time were arming the people, this applies to the SDA, the SDS, and the HDZ, and that within that framework, preparations were being engaged in for what they called the defence of their own people. That is my knowledge regarding the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you say that it was -- that this was a generally known matter in late 1991, early 1992, that the Patriotic League existed and that people were being armed in preparation for an armed conflict within this Patriotic League? Was that a generally known thing?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many generally known things. This one among others.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And just give me your best impression. Were these arming activities going on independently of each other, between the various groups, or was the arming that went on among the Serbs a reaction to what was going on in the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All sides were arming themselves in great haste. Mostly out of fear of one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You talked yesterday in response to some questions from Ms. Korner about discipline within the ranks of the SDS, and you told us that someone who openly disagreed with SDS policy would be punished and termed a traitor and disciplined in some way. Can you name anyone, and specifically from the Krajina area, who was disciplined because of their disagreement with SDS policy?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those days, or generally speaking for the whole period?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In those days, I'm talking about late 1991 and through the fall of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that the SDS was a compact, well-structured organisation in which the hierarchy was respected. And I do know that differing views, even though they wanted to present themselves as a democratic party, were not really tolerated, especially not at that time. And still less was their tolerance for behaviour that could be interpreted as not being in conformity with the policy of the party. I can't remember a single name but there were many people in the past who were in the SDS and because they acted differently, they left the party. I think that Mr. Brdjanin himself left the SDS later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We talked yesterday about Brdjanin's continuing starting, starting very early on and continuing opposition to Pale regarding where the seat of government should be, and his continual opposition to Pale in that regard. And you just mentioned what I was getting ready to ask you. He was, in fact, kicked out of parliament and kicked out of the party, was he not, for his complaining in the parliament about war profiteering?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Correct. But I think Mr. Brdjanin left the party himself, but I'm not sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. In fact, he wound up forming his own party, didn't he, at one point?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want you to look at an exhibit that you saw yesterday, and just ask you some questions about it, it's P117. Now, I don't know if you've had a chance, Mr. Dodik, to actually read this entire document or if you've just been directed to various parts of it. But the question I have for you is this: On 27 February, 1992, an interview is being conducted of Mr. Brdjanin and Mr. Krajisnik. Krajisnik at that time was probably one of the top three most powerful people in the SDS. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a strong man of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And would you also agree that what was going on in this interview was in many ways a dispute between Brdjanin and Krajisnik where Brdjanin is disagreeing with him and he's disagreeing with Brdjanin about two or three matters?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't managed to read the whole text of the interview because it's a poor photocopy, but in any event, yes, it is visible that views differed, their views differed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And Brdjanin was in effect in this public interview of 27 February, 1992, diverging from the SDS line and the SDS policy, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That can be seen in the positions that are reviewed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, Karadzic came to Banja Luka to discipline the Banja Luka organisation, and after that, the organisation came under the direct control of the top leadership in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you know when that was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it was around those days and months, maybe May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Even after, even after Karadzic visited Banja Luka, Brdjanin continued to agitate about the seat of government being in Banja Luka and continued to oppose Pale in that regard, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that this was a continuous effort on his part throughout those years.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Ms. Korner asked you yesterday why Brdjanin was made president of the Crisis Staff instead of Kupresanin, and I think what you told us was that you really didn't know. Let me ask you the other side of that question: Do you know why Kupresanin was made president of the ARK assembly instead of Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said earlier on that I was not a part of those structures. I can just assume that this was part of an agreement among them, and I think that it wouldn't have been possible otherwise, but I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you aware that there was a great deal of opposition to Brdjanin from some of the more powerful municipalities that were part of ARK? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of the Sanska Unska group of municipalities and their efforts to get Mr. Brdjanin replaced as head of the Crisis Staff by Mr. Kupresanin? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about that specifically, but I do know that there was some kind of an informal group that operated informally. And I think that the MPs from those municipalities acted in a homogenous manner and they acted homogenously in various places.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's the next thing I wanted to discuss with you actually, so we have got a good introduction into it. You told us yesterday about strong local individuals, and you mentioned in Prijedor Mr. Drljaca. And I'm wondering if you're aware of some others who were strong individuals. I'm wondering if you would feel that way about Gojko Klickovic, for instance, in Krupa?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Practically every municipality had a clearly distinguishable strong individual. In Bosanska Krupa, in addition to Gojko Klickovic, it was also MP Vijestica. And in Sanski Most, for example, a strong individual was Mr. Rasula.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How about Kljuc? Do you know anybody there that had that kind of a position?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was someone, but I can't remember the name now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would I be wrong in concluding that what you're really saying to this Trial Chamber about what happened in late 1991 and 1992 in terms of the lines of authority was that it was based more on personality than it was on structure? For instance, many of these powerful persons in these municipalities were persons who had a very close relationship with Karadzic and would naturally deal directly with Karadzic rather than with someone like Kupresanin or Brdjanin? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to say that at local levels, there were strong individuals who comprised this strong structure of the party. And I can confirm that these people attached greater importance to Karadzic and his authority than they would have attached to anyone at regional level.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want to finally ask you about four camps: Omarska, Keraterm, Trnopolje and Manjaca. Now, the first three that I've mentioned, Omarska, Keraterm, Trnopolje, those three were all located within the Prijedor municipality, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters could not understand the answer. Could the witness please be asked to speak up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Could you repeat your answer because the interpreters didn't catch up with you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a well-known thing. These places do belong to the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you aware, did you ever become aware, that Manjaca was termed at least a prisoner of war camp and operated exclusively by the military, the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the media, there were situations in which a large number of members of the Croatian Army were arrested and sent to Manjaca. A few days later or in that period, there was a convoy, a large convoy of buses who -- that drove these people from Manjaca to Croatia and they went through the place where I lived. And that's how I was aware of these buses. I don't know how many buses were involved but it was known at the time that these were people who had been at Manjaca and that they were now being transferred to Croatia. They were not only Croatian soldiers, there were probably others involved as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My question, though, was: Were you aware that Manjaca was under control of the 1st Krajina Corps and run as an army POW camp?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that you first learned about the existence of various camps when Mr. Kouchner came to Banja Luka to investigate press reports about the existence of the camps. My question is, I'm sure you don't know the exact date but it would have had to have been after the existence of the camps was publicised in the international press, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was Mr. Kouchner. When he came to the airport then, it was said and I confirmed it yesterday, that he said that there were certain indications, that there was a camp there, and that he came to talk to the authorities in that region in Banja Luka, in Prijedor, about this. I know that he was met by Mr. Vukic at the airport at the time, as a representative of the authorities. After that, I don't know anything what happened. I just heard that there was the possibility of the existence of some camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He specifically mentioned that he was there because of press reports regarding the camps, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He said that media in the west were saying that he came on behalf of the Doctors without Borders or some other organisation to check these allegations. And I've already said that I was there when he came but afterwards I was not with him at all, so I don't know anything about that, whether he actually established this to be a fact or not. I really don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And as you told us yesterday, the real specific details about these camps you only learned after the war was over. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: During those early months of 1992, May, June, July, the existence of those camps was not a generally known thing, was not something that people were talking about, or to your knowledge, knew about, generally?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't discussed very much. You have to bear in mind that local communities were quite isolated from one another, so many things that were going on in Prijedor were things that people didn't know about in the place where I lived. There was a psychosis of fear and of impending war and of course there were a lot of rumours that were going around, but I told you when I first heard of this. I don't know. I've never been there myself. I never went even after the war. But my knowledge in this respect is linked to this visit paid by Mr. Kouchner at the time. At assemblies where I was present, there was no mention of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Don't you think that Drljaca and other authorities in Prijedor involved in this would have wanted to keep the existence of those Prijedor camps a secret? Don't you think that's what they would have wanted to do?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot interpret their intentions. I never spoke to them. I've already said what the situation was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at an exhibit, P1237, please. Sir, this is a document dated 31 May of 1992 from the public security station Prijedor, and it appears to have been signed by Simo Drljaca. And I want to draw your attention to a few parts of it. I think the first part that is of interest is the first paragraph. "With a view to the speedy and effective establishment of peace on the territory of Prijedor municipality, and in accordance with the decision of the Crisis Staff, I hereby order the following." And then there is a list of things that are ordered by Drljaca and specifically I'd like you to look at paragraphs 13, 15 and 16. The document basically sets up and creates the camp at Omarska at the Omarska mine, and so the paragraphs 13, 15, and 16 relate to that. Paragraph 13 says that: "All authorised officials who have been assigned duties at this collection centre or related to it shall observe the positive legislation and rules of service, in particular they must keep official secrets and protect the property in their charge." Then if you look at 15, he becomes more explicit about that: "I most strictly prohibit giving any information whatsoever concerning the functioning of this collection centre. All official documents shall be kept at the collection centre and may be taken out or destroyed only with the permission of the chief of the Prijedor public security station. This shall be the responsibility of the security staff." And then finally in 16, he says: "I demand most energetically that all the personnel and authorised officials in particular strictly observe these instructions. Failure to do so shall result in severe disciplinary and other measures." Now, clearly, this was an effort on behalf of Drljaca to keep secret the Omarska camp, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course this is the first time I see this document. Of course, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the English and French transcripts. I don't wish or want to speak about its authenticity. I cannot check that. I've already said that I cannot make any comments in this regard. But on the basis of what is written here, it is clearly stated that what was prohibited was prohibited in item 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And with regard to what you've said about the position of Mr. Drljaca, his powerful position, it would have not been wise for persons to ignore his directive regarding the keeping of this secret and to ignore his warning that failure to do so would result in severe disciplinary and other measures, would it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That can be seen from what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Dodik, I want to thank you so much for coming here and trying to help us understand some of the issues in this case. I hope you have a pleasant trip home, and I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Ms. Korner has -- is going to re-examine you on some issues raised during Mr. Ackerman's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodik, yesterday, in answer to questions by Mr. Ackerman, you quoted, as so many others have, the sentence of Mr. Izetbegovic that he was ready to sacrifice peace in Bosnia for an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina. Who was going to disturb the peace, Mr. Dodik?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand the question, but in my opinion, peace was disturbed then by the ruling nationalist parties that were speedily arming everyone and pursuing the kind of policy that led to an armed conflict. Mr. Karadzic's speeches in parliament in those days in those times are well known and at one point he said that if there is a war, the entire Muslim nation could disappear or something like that. And at the same time, this statement made by Mr. Izetbegovic was made as well. The representatives of the Croat political parties were not lagging behind in this respect either. They were creating such an atmosphere that it was impossible to pinpoint one single perpetrator, at least in my opinion, everybody, all the representatives of the then national oligarchies had a hand in this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I was about to ask you, were you present on the 15th of October, when Mr. Karadzic made his speech to the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was present.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When he said to the assembly, to the Muslims, the Croats, "Please take it seriously. It is not good what you are doing. This is the road you want Bosnia and Herzegovina to take, the same highway of hell and suffering that Slovenia and Croatia went through. Don't think you won't take Bosnia and Herzegovina to hell and the Muslim people to possible extinction. Because the Muslim people will not be able to defend itself if it comes to war." Do you remember those words?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that speech made by Mr. Karadzic but I do not remember every single word, of course. I do know though that he spoke to that effect, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the fact was, wasn't it, that the Muslims and Croats wanted the referendum on independence and the Serbs didn't?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a fact. You have to bear in mind that already then, there was significant fighting in Croatia, in the end of 1991 there was quite literally a war that was being waged in Croatia and this had a considerable influence over the behaviour of quite a few people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is correct, though, that some wanted the referendum and others did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's concentrate on the question I asked. The Croats and Muslims, as we saw in February of 1992, voted in favour of independence. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They voted -- I mean, are you referring to the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm referring now to the actual referendum that was held.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The referendum, yes. Yes. That was the outcome that was made public.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it was always clear, wasn't it, to you and to the SDS that if a referendum was held, the Muslims and Croats would vote in favour of independent Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was clear, when the decision was made in order to have this referendum organised. I already said that the representatives of the Bosniaks and the Croats in parliament were in favour of the referendum, whereas the representatives of the Serbs were not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the threats to disturb the peace that Mr. Izetbegovic was talking about came entirely from the SDS, through Mr. -- Dr. Karadzic, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I think that in different ways and at different levels, everybody contributed to that. That is to say, to disturbing the peace, namely the SDS, the SDA and the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know that's what you said, Mr. Dodik, but I'm asking you, isn't the reality that the only threats to disturb the peace in Bosnia were coming from the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not my experience of it and I don't think that's the way it was. I think it was the way I put it earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said to Mr. Ackerman yesterday that the Serbs -- let me just put to you the exact words you used -- page 53, "most Serbs in those days considered it to be quite normal that they should be in the community of Serbia as the motherland and that the form of order for Bosnia-Herzegovina should be such that it should remain in a community in a -- in an agreed community with Serbia and the other republics wishing to remain within Yugoslavia." By the end of 1991, the only republics left in Yugoslavia were Serbia, and Montenegro and Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And so the desire -- I'm sorry, you wanted to say something else?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- what was said yesterday had to be corrected in the transcript, so I want to say it once again. At that time in the end of 1991, at least this was my experience and that's why I joined the parliament of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Bosnia-Herzegovina was supposed to be redefined and there should be a new agreement among the political factors in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In Bosnia-Herzegovina together with the other republics, primarily with Serbia, was supposed to stay on in some kind of a community that would be a continuation of Yugoslavia. Serbs did feel that Serbia was their motherland but I have to say once again that I'm convinced that by the end of 1991, there were obvious attempts made in Bosnia-Herzegovina to seek an alliance with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. That's all I'm asking you, Mr. Dodik. Effectively the desire to remain in Yugoslavia expressed by the Serbs was a desire to remain with Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And other republics who wished to do so. Montenegro, at that time people were counting on Macedonia too, that it would go through a process that would definitely end in Macedonia's joining that union too. There are well-known attempts that were made in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you told -- Mr. Ackerman was asking you about Mr. Brdjanin yesterday, this is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think my LiveNote is out, so to coincide with Mr. Ackerman's it would be page 60, that you were asked what you meant by your answer that you and Brdjanin were in conflict, and you said, "We were in different political parties, that's the conflict I meant." And you were then asked you were just speaking of the fact that you were in different parties -- that were you in a different party from him and you said, "Yes, and we had different political organisations and therefore we had different views regarding certain matters." Can I ask on what matters you and Mr. Brdjanin had different views, please?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday and I can confirm today, that the party that I belonged to believed that negotiations should be persisted upon and that a certain solution should be found at the green table, as it is usually put, Pages blanches insérées aux fins d’assurer la correspondance entre la pagination anglaise et la pagination française. and that this was the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At that time, the SDS pursued a different policy, and it was obvious that through the formation of regional organisations, they wished to pursue that and we as a party disagreed with that. We thought that the situation should not be made even more troublesome, that an agreement should be reached on the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina and then the restructuring of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was the main point. Also we as a party advocated the preservation of Yugoslavia. When we realised that was no longer possible, then as you could see from the documents that were presented yesterday, a group of people and I left this party and we tried to be politically rational and loyal and in this way to contribute to stabilisation as much as possible and also to averting the danger of a war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that's a long answer, sir, and I'm not sure it is an answer to the question that I asked. You say that they pursued a different policy, that is to say, the SDS, and it was obvious through the regional -- I think you said the creation of regional organisations they wished to pursue that and we disagreed with that. What was the different policy? What was the creation of the regional organisations symptomatic of?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, symptomatic or not, it meant a new structure within Bosnia-Herzegovina itself. On the one hand, it was supported. On the other hand, it was not supported. For example, the idea of an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina was not supported by the Serbs. So this only made the situation even more complicated and we thought, we as a party, thought that we should abstain, that everybody should be abstain from any kind of new solutions that would complicate the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina even further.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. You still haven't answered the question. What in your view was the purpose of the creation of these regional organisations?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that I answered that question yesterday. I said that this was a reaction in the conditions in which people lived, namely there was already a war in Croatia and also in Krajina, and it was motivated by these developments, at least that's how it was presented in public. That is to say, organising the Serb people in these areas. On the other hand, I said that this constituted a new political, territorial segment in the very existence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that was promoted by the SDS. However it was not accepted by the SDA and the HDZ. Also, likewise, the concept of independent Bosnia-Herzegovina was not espoused by the SDS, and I cannot give a more precise answer than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, you see, do you remember saying at an earlier stage, when you were seen, that the purpose was for the regional institutions to gather the municipalities together, where the Serbs were a minority, or where they belonged, Serbs gathered to protect themselves?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were a majority and in some municipalities where they were a minority, joined these communities later, at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm sorry, sir, I know you say this is what the setting up of the regions was because of what happened in Croatia but what I want to know is what was the part about the setting up of these regional organisations that you as a party or you personally disapproved of?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't agree because that was another step contributing to the complexity of the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We didn't agree because as I said those regional organisations were not supported by everyone and they were an additional cause of conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why were they an additional cause of conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the concept of the SDA and the HDZ was a unitary Bosnia and Herzegovina and they wanted to promote such a structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas on the other hand, SDS wanted a decentralised Bosnia-Herzegovina and tried to set up those institutions. I shall come back to another assertion I made that we felt at the time that that should not have been done as it further complicated the situation. Both the concepts of regionalisation and the unitary concept. These were concepts that could not find approval throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to have one last go at this. Is your objection that there was another level of authority being set up on a regional basis which detracted from the authority, as you call it the unitary authority, the authority of the republican government?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was certainly a new segment in the territorial political structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina that had authority in BH, but it is highly questionable to what extent the authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina had legitimacy as they were not supported by everyone in Bosnia-Herzegovina, all the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now I want to deal with a couple of other matters. You were asked about saying that Brdjanin was, as you put it, crazy, and he was the public -- "he took our public face. Radic conducted the policy. That's why the international community went to where the power was, Radic." And then you said this: "Had Banja Luka acted differently, then the Serbs would have acted differently." Now, do you agree that's something that you said?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most part, yes, but that Banja Luka would have behaved differently, that the Serbs would have behaved differently is not true. What I said was that the Banja Luka is the largest municipality in the region and had it had a different policy, a certain number of the smaller municipalities around it might have pursued a different policy, too. As for this attribute of crazy, I said that it should be put in quotation marks. He accepted public responsibility but my opinion was that he was part of a collective body, he represented that body, and he made public appearances only on behalf of that body.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. As far as you were asked about him leaving parliament, when did that happen? Can you remember, roughly? And setting up his own party.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it did happen, but I can't actually pinpoint the time. I think it was later on, maybe, in the fourth or fifth year. I know that he had a party at the first multi-party elections which he was a president, and it was called the People's Party of Republika Srpska. I mean the first post-war elections.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I was going to say, is that after Dayton?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that it appeared and took part at the first elections after Dayton. Those were the only elections. It couldn't have taken part in any elections before that, there weren't any.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Were you aware that he became a vice-president of the Republika Srpska, in September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Vice-president?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vice-president of Republika Srpska, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Vice-president or Deputy Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I always get confused between these terms. I think vice-president. I think it's a vice-president as opposed to Deputy Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you aware of that, Mr. Dodik?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that he was vice-president of the republic but I did know that he was in the government. I don't know. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe in some other situation, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The final matter that I want to ask you about is something you've just been asked about now and that's the camps. Do you remember telling us about an incident, telling the investigator, in the taped interview with you, ten days ago or whenever it was, about an incident when Kupresanin took a man out of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is at page 14.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember. Mr. Kupresanin, at one of the assembly meetings appeared with --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to this. This is completely new matter. It's not a response to anything that I did on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: She is going into a whole new subject matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: About Mr. Kupresanin and what he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't agree with you, Mr. Ackerman, because your question to him was directed into the witness confirming that Manjaca, for example, was completely and exclusively administered and run by the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I, just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman suggested to the witness that Omarska was totally secret and that nobody, including this witness, knew about it until Mr. Kouchner arrived. That's why I'm re-examining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's even more clear. I don't see your objection, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it has nothing to do with Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But if she is now going to raise this issue then I should be permitted to cross-examine on it because I didn't have an opportunity to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's see what the question and answer is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Because it really ask a whole new subject matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I think it arises from your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I make it as plain and simple as I possibly can? Mr. Ackerman spent the last ten minutes of his cross-examination explaining just how secret Omarska was, that nobody would dare to breathe a word of it in the light of Simo Drljaca's order. This goes directly to that issue as to how secret it actually was. And that effectively --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, now, Mr. Dodik, I'm sorry about that interruption, can you tell us about the incident where Mr. Kupresanin took someone out of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You said from Omarska. At the time I didn't know it was a camp. This happened as follows: At a parliament session in Banja Luka, Mr. Kupresanin addressed me and a number of other deputies, claiming that near Banja Luka, in the Vrbanja settlement, there was a deputy from the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina whose name I now cannot recall, and who had come from Omarska, and who wanted to join in the work of the parliament of Republika Srpska. I must say that I spoke to that man, together with Mr. Kupresanin. He was obviously in fear this could -- this was visible. But after that conversation, I really don't know what happened. And I have to confirm that the man did come from Omarska but at the time I didn't know that it was any kind of camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, did Mr. Kupresanin tell you that this man was coming from Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did, that he had come from Omarska, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did he tell you what Omarska was? Forget about that it was a camp or a camp in the sense that we now know it was, but did he tell you what it was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly what he said, but I think that in those days, it was seen as a place where Bosniaks were being gathered, and I think he said he had been there but I cannot confirm that with precision. I didn't enter into the gist of it. He probably approached me, knowing my positions and knowing that I would agree to talk to that man, and in that conversation, there was no mention of Omarska as a camp. He was a deputy from Prijedor municipality. I don't know exactly from which location, whether it was from Prijedor or from Omarska or from some other village. I can just say that Mr. Kupresanin did say that the man had come from Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you tell the investigator that there had been rumours going around about Omarska? About the collection centre?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were rumours in those days, and I said that today again, there were many rumours, many reports confirmed and unconfirmed that were being spread about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you also tell the investigator that it was because Kupresanin took a Muslim from Omarska that he fell out of favour with the SDS, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was part of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dodik. That's all that I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, based upon the last part I do have some additional cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you want to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to ask about this whole issue about Kupresanin and Omarska and the person that was taken out because that did not come up in the direct examination, so I didn't get a chance to cross-examine about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but Mr. Ackerman took the line which was in our view a line that couldn't possibly be supported by this part of the evidence. I wouldn't have dealt with it otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you have brought up another matter in the wake of your question, Ms. Korner, namely that the fact that Mr. Kupresanin was instrumental in bringing or taking this person out of Omarska marked the beginning of his downfall.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I accept that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So on the basis of that I'm allowing Mr. Ackerman to take that point up and cross-examine the witness further. That's only about that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I only have about two or three questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope so, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It will be very quick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not going to allow you to start your cross-examination again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it will be very quick.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Dodik, as I understand, and please correct me if I misunderstand, what you were told about this person was that he had come from Omarska, not necessarily from some kind of a camp in Omarska, but just from Omarska, is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the other thing that you said was that the fact that Mr. Kupresanin had basically brought a Muslim and suggested that a Muslim become part of the Assembly of Republika Srpska, become a deputy in that assembly, representing the Prijedor municipality, was the beginning of Mr. Kupresanin's downfall within the SDS organisation. I think that was also your position, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: For that reason, among others, Mr. Kupresanin was out of favour later on, not just for that reason but probably that was one of the reasons. It's my opinion. I can't go into the internal relationships within the SDS. This is just my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever hear or do you have any knowledge whatsoever about the proposition that Mr. Kupresanin in this instance was operating under directions from Mr. Karadzic to try to bring a Muslim into the RS assembly because Mr. Karadzic believed that would be helpful in his international negotiations? Did you ever hear that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something like that did not happen later on, so I can't claim that that was true. I had the impression that this was a personal act by Mr. Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one question that I think I should ask in private session, then I'll be finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman is going to repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just have to repeat the question because the question is not in the record at this point or not in the public record, the person that Mr. Kupresanin brought to Banja Luka that you had an opportunity to talk to, do you recall that his name was Mevludin Sejmenovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all I have, thank you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. There are no questions from the Bench or the Chamber. Which basically means that your testimony comes to an end here. Which also means that you're free to go back to your home. You will be assisted by the officers of this Tribunal in all you need to enable you to make your return easy. On behalf of Judge Janu from the Czech Republic and Judge Taya who is not with us today, from Japan and, of course, on my own behalf and on behalf of the Tribunal, I should like to thank you sir for having come over to give testimony in this trial against Radoslav Brdjanin and I wish to join Mr. Ackerman and I'm sure I will be expressing the wishes of everyone present in this room, I wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, and Mr. Ackerman, shall we break now?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I was going to suggest that, Your Honour and then we can deal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It doesn't make sense starting now and breaking after ten minutes if we are not going to conclude in ten minutes. So we will have a 25 minute break and then hopefully we should conclude in one hour or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this is what's called housekeeping with a vengeance. Your Honours should have in front of you an index to the documents we want to deal with this morning. On top is the item index, and underneath you will see detailed index to some of the documents we want to deal with. Your Honour, can I first of all deal with what's item number 1 on this list, which is documents which are records of the Serbian assembly? They have all been put together in I think two binders, three binders, and some of them we wanted them put together as a collection. Some have already been exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have not checked beforehand whether I have enough room in my Chamber because I'm running short of space very rapidly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you're like us, Your Honour, we have all got them along the corridor. We fight for the space in the cupboards. Your Honour, we have indicated very clearly those that are already exhibited, for example, P21 in the second set of schedules and those that are new documents and we would like to have exhibited, Your Honours, from -- starting with Exhibit number 2463. And so can I formally ask Your Honours to admit those into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman, I suppose, I get the usual response from you and then I will proceed with pronouncing the usual order or decision. So, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I was just handed this whole list, just moments ago, and so I'm not in any position to make much of a response at this point, other than to say I probably have objections to a number of these but I can't possibly formulate them at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are formal records, as we've already seen and we went through with Mr. Dodik of the assemblies, it's got nothing to do with AID or anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He is not saying that he definitely has objections, that he may have objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, this is the point and this is the difficulty, of course, because with the speeded up, as it were, schedule, we will be relying on quite a number of these documents for the purposes of the Rule 98 brief. So it's perhaps important that if there is to be an objection, Mr. Ackerman puts that in in writing before we get to the actual filing of these briefs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that does not create a problem, Ms. Korner, because for the purposes of the Rule 98 bis decision, we don't go into credibility and authenticity, unless it is a clear-cut case of a forged document which goes beyond any reasonable doubt at all. So yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, for the purposes of the record right now, without having had an opportunity to actually go through this very much, I'm going to object to each and every one of these on the grounds that they are being offered way too late in this process. If you look at these lists, these documents were acquired by OTP some as early as 1994, some 1998, 1995, 1998, 1995. Surely the Prosecutor has known for some time that they wanted to use these and could certainly have made that known to the Defence in time for the Defence to make some kind of a rational response to them. That's not been done. I mean, we have rules about disclosure and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to stop --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- Listing exhibits briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I stop Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They have been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They have all been disclosed about two years ago, we think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which is the whole point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, then that's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But I was waiting here for you to finish because I knew exactly what to expect from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I move them into evidence subject to any objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's obvious.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how we have proceeded all along, and that's how we will continue to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next item number 2 is a set of documents which we would ask to be moved into evidence as 2492 to -- until P2517, which are all documents which relate to the issue of international armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, Your Honours, the next -- and they are listed in full on the index attached to the front index, as it were. Your Honour, then thereafter there are new documents relating to the Banja Luka municipality and the documents relating to Bosanski Novi. Those are documents that literally arrived in the last few weeks, as far as Bosanski Novi is concerned, as a result of personal request to the municipality to hand over documents, despite, as I think I pointed out to Your Honour at the time, a series of letters to the Republika Srpska asking for these documents which bore no result. Your Honour, thereafter we have put in documents which relate to Mr. Brown's report, which obviously Mr. Ackerman will want to see for his cross-examination. Documents supporting the exhumation schedules. Again, some documents relating to the police is the next item, and some further translations of newspaper articles. Item number 9 is one new document relating to the Petrovac municipality. It was one of the ones produced by Mr. Hidic which wasn't actually used but it's a report on the SDS. Your Honour, there are further documents relating to Prijedor, to Prnjavor, a general section relating to the Republika Srpska and the SA-- SDS, a document relating to Sipovo, new documents relating to Teslic, as a result of the same procedure, namely that there was a personal visit to the municipality by an investigator. Your Honour, the next item, videos and transcripts, that is just checking whether that includes-- no. That all relate to the area in which we haven't yet formally exhibited. Your Honour, there are some additional photographs relating to the municipalities of Banja Luka, Sanski Most, and Kljuc. Now, Your Honour, item 17, may I just give a little explanation for that? Your Honours will recall a very long time ago in this case a witness was cross-examined on the basis that having asserted that Mrs. Brdjanin worked for something called GIK Kozara, it was put to him and documents were listed showing that it was a different company. Your Honour, the documents we have acquired, we suggest, show that the company which Mrs. Brdjanin worked for was in fact part of GIK Kozara. So that's what those documents relate to. And Your Honour, I think for that one, we haven't given it a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, you haven't, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in fact, not only that, Ms. Korner but all the subsequent items -- exhibits, from item 17 right through 32 with the exception of item 30.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's because we weren't entirely sure whether we were going to be putting any more exhibits in with Mr. Dodik. Your Honour, I'm asking if that -- if a note could be made on the schedule that that one be made P2642. That's item 17 on the schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 2642. Okay. I see that it consists of one, two, three, four different documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They've all been put together, Your Honour n one single bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. 18?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Does Your Honour have that document there? Because I can show Your Honours why we say that. It's the one -- oh, they don't, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's going to be handed in at the end of all of this. Don't worry. Now, Your Honour, item number 18, the report relating to Rasula's diary. Now, I don't know whether that particular issue has now been as it were discarded because it was actually raised by Ms. Fauveau in respect of the Defence for General Talic. Your Honour, we have that report from the graphologist in Kiev. I'm afraid it took a little time to try and sort all the matters out which related to it. Your Honour, in essence, perhaps I can put it this way: And I'm going to summarise what the report shows so I'm not giving evidence, it's just a summary because it's quite a lengthy report. That the diary was definitely in their view written by Rasula. They had comparison of known writings from Rasula and there's statements attached from the various investigators who provided the material. There are two entries in Cyrillic written by someone else. One on the 22nd of October, 1990, so way beyond the period, and on the 3rd of November, 1990. Neither of these entries were considered relevant. Nobody asked any questions about it. But those two entries, there are two entries there written by someone else. Your Honour, as far as the -- there are Latin script entries, leaving aside what we discovered was somebody having written over the top of the Cyrillic was, when Your Honours may recall when we found the original diary were not present on the original but there are two Latin script entries which the handwriting expert was unable to determine the authorship of because there was insufficient Latin script for Rasula, by Rasula, provided for comparison. Again they both relate to 1990. The 3rd of October, 1990 and the 20th of October, 1990. Your Honour, as far as Ms. Fauveau's objection was concerned, there is on, I think, there was one page that she objected to, and I think we'll find that she originally objected because it was the Latin script written over the top, which as I say we found that was not on the original, and the actual page on which this Latin script appeared, the handwriting experts judged to be Rasula's writing. Your Honour, the only other complication to that is this: That we will have to produce a third version of the report because Your Honours may recall that the copies that had the ERN numbers were two pages copied on one page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The handwriting said they wanted it separately so there is a third version of it, I'm sorry, so that will have to be exhibited separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I don't remember, Ms. Korner, is whether at the time Mr. Ackerman had joined with the Defence of General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think he did, but I'll let Mr. Ackerman speak for himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With Madam Fauveau, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I did too, Your Honour, but I don't remember for certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps -- all right. It's okay. But I invite you to look into this, to see whether you maintain your position in that case. So let's proceed. We would give or you propose to give this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: P2643, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Together with...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The diary, the new version of the diary which will be 2643.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next item, number 19, is the statement showing what documents were given and how they were acquired, so may that be made -- Mr. Grady's statement will be P2644.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dupas, 2645.
